raw_comment:
Looking at this graph, I can see all the state's favorite Thanksgiving side dishes. I can see how these traditional side dishes vary. I find it interesting that there are so many different food favorites in different states. I had never heard of cookie salad or pig pickin cake, nor frog eye salad. 

I wonder why some of these meals are so obscure, like the frog eye salad. That's pasta, pineapple, coconut and mandarin oranges? Topped with cream? I mean, that seems a little strange. But it's not my state, so I don’t know. 

Where I am from, NC, it's usually just mashed potatoes and green bean casserole. I’ve never even had pig pickin cake. 
My favorite side dishes have always been the same, to be honest. Buttery, creamed mashed potatoes and homemade baked mac and cheese. Those two things with a big turkey slice are the best on thanksgiving. I also adore pecan pie, it's heavenly with a scoop of French vanilla ice cream.

raw_comment: Looking at this graph taken from a TheUpshot article, you can see the mundane cultural differences in people’s favorite side dishes. Arizona residents add an ethnic twist to the classic turkey dish, with the most popular side being turkey enchiladas. There’s also aspects in these favored dishes that just show the agricultural traits of states, for example California’s San Joaquin Valley produces loads of yams as a popular organic ‘superfood’, with which state’s residents use to make persimmon bread. I don’t know how I’ve never heard of any of these dishes or foods, and honestly I’ve never heard of the favored dish in my own state. “Pig pickin’ cake”, North Carolina’s apparent favorite, is a fruity dessert that came from pig barbecues in the south. There’s yellow cake, mandarin, oranges and whipped cream to fill in the layers and topped with pecans as well as vanilla pudding. When I hear about this dessert I think of my grandma, who’s totally an old jello and circus peanut salad fashioned kind of woman, but I guess she just stuck with the ambrosia salad over the orange nutty cake with time.

Title: Thanksgiving peculiar side dishes in each state

This thanksgiving dish map is very peculiar as I don't I know or even heard of a singly dish on there. Maybe I might be uncultured in what America actually eats on thanksgiving but i think other people can also relate. I noticed that some foods  such as different types of salad; snicker salad, fruit salad, frog eye salad, and cookie salad, have a top mid portion hearth in the U.S around the states North and South Dakota, and Montana.  Different assortments of pie are also common along the north east. The state in which I am living in also has a dish called "stuffed artichokes" which I've never heard of before or even seen how the dish looks like. Frog eye salad seems to be prominent in the mid western part of the U.S and my only question is what weirdo would search up "frog eye salad" and actually try it. This map also slightly hints at how culturally diverse the population. The only dish that I would actually be excited to try would be the smoked salmon drip; just for my vitamin D deficiency:) It also sound delicious and I prefer savory and umami flavors rather than sweet or sour.

raw_comment: I noticed that all the thanksgiving foods people have can range from healthy vegan main dishes or side dishes, or sugary and sweet desserts. I think a name for this graph could be: Have You Eaten Your States' Food For Thanksgiving?

What’s Going On in This Graph? | November 18, 2020

What is the most “distinct” Thanksgiving side dish in Ohio? What is that?
The most distinct Thanksgiving side dish in Ohio is dirt pudding. 



Write one to two complete sentences for the first 3 questions

What do you notice?
What I notice is that every state has a different unusually popular food and there is really no dish that repeats in a geographical area, it is scattered. What I also notice is that Ohio is the only state with dirt pudding. 





What do you wonder?
What I wonder is what some of these dishes are that I have never heard of. What I also wonder is how they found this data. 





What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impact it has on my community is that people near me like certain foods that I like too. It also has an impact for my community to try new foods this year. 




Write a catchy headline for the last question

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Unusually foods

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  “Pass the Frog Eye Salad, Please!" by F from Perkins School for the Blind in Watertown, Massachusetts; "Not Your Average Thanksgiving Meal" by Abigail of Georgia; “Gobble Up Some of These Delicious Dishes” by Hayden of Valley Stream North High School in New York: and "From Dirt Pudding to Turkey:  Explore the Variety Within the U.S." by Rodolfo, "Giving Thanks....and Food” by Aboubakary, and "What's On America's Plate This Thanksgiving?" by Cass, all from New York City.


You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Nov. 20, to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I notice that pies are very popular in the New England states. For instance, pumpkin woopie pie is enjoyed in both Maine and Vermont, Maple Walnut Pie is a favorite in New Hampshire, and chocolate cream pie is a popular dish in Rhode Island. In addition, I notice that both New Mexico and Florida’s most popular dishes seem to have Hispanic influence. Lastly, I notice that Frog Eye Salad is a favorite dish in the Far West states of Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Colorado, and Nevada. 

What do you wonder? 
How were these dishes created? How have different ethnic groups influenced these dishes? How have foods grown in certain areas influenced the type of side dishes eaten in there? 

What impact does this have on you? 
The impact that it has on me is that now I want to try these dishes, especially Asparagus Casserole and Sweet Potato Dumplings, which both sound delicious and most less-unusual. My home state of Delaware’s favorite unusual side dish is pretzel salad and now I really want to try that too.

raw_comment:
I notice that side dishes vary greatly, but some states do share the same side dish. Frog eye salad and snicker salad seem to be popular in the Midwest/West. I haven't heard of many of these dishes before. Some states have simpler and more usual side dishes though, such as VA with collard green, MI with cheesy potatoes, and NY with stuffed artichokes. I noticed that pie seems to be common within New England, while salads are more common in the Midwest/West. 

I wonder if these side dishes have to do with the location. Based on location, these foods could be something that is suitable for the weather during Thanksgiving or the agricultural/typical foods that are found within that area. I wonder why these dishes are popular in each state and how they originated. Since many of the foods on the western side of the map are unfamiliar to me, I wonder if someone from the West Coast would be familiar with any of the dishes on the eastern side of the map. 

This impacts my community because it shows the different foods that we eat and how we diversify what is considered to be a common culture. In addition, although I'm from MA, I'm not sure if I can say that I've eaten mashed butternut squash - or even squash in general - at Thanksgiving.

A possible headline could be "Try These States' Unusual Side Dishes at Your Thanksgiving Table This Year"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The food being mentioned in the graphs, some are somewhat reasonable when it comes to their "unusualness" but some are very interesting and uncommon. Chocolate cream pie, cheesy potatoes or fruit salad, even though not commonly eat in Thanksgiving, are very easy to understand when it comes to their popularity. However, some food mentioned in the graph like frog eye salad, snicker/cookie salad, or funeral potatoes are food that some would even consider "weird". The graph show a wide range of food selection from salad, pudding, casserole, pie, cheesecake to potato dishes. Many dishes are the combination of different senses and flavor of sweet and salty, creating a very diverse range of food.

What do you wonder? 
How were these food created? Where was it originated? Why it is popular? especially in Thanksgiving? Who popularized them?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I have been to Washington State and stayed there for 2 years. I can confirmed that smoked salmon dip is in fact famous there. The graph shows many kind of different but interesting food, making me wanting to try all of it, inspire me to visit all of these states to try these "unusually popular" dishes. Though some food being mentioned are somewhat strange, it is a way to unite people coming from the same state.

Headline: Frog eye salad! Funeral potato! Pig pickin cake! - the unusually popular dishes around the nation during Thanksgiving!

raw_comment:
On this graph, I notice all of the different and similar most popular food recipes according to the states. It is very interesting to see how many states go for a side to eat at the actual part of dinner and who chooses to go for the dessert portion for the night. One thing that really stuck out to me was the frog eye salad, the fact that it popped up twice on the map is so mind-boggling because I never even associated frog with Thanksgiving. I think it is very interesting how many different options and sides that people choose to eat at Thanksgiving, especially the ones that you wouldn't have thought of because of your geographical placement in the United States. I wonder why there is not a single this googled for plain mashed potatoes because people can make those so many different ways. This is very interesting to me because depending on where my community or I go for thanksgiving we could have very different main course sides. 

Headline: "The United State's Most popular Sides on Thanksgiving!!"

raw_comment:
What I Noticed

- I noticed that several recipes had odd names, such as frog eye salad and pretzel salad, that didn’t quite match with what they actually looked like or were composed of..
- Many states had foods that I had never thought of when I thought about Thanksgiving, which seemed interesting.
- I also noticed that most foods on this graph were desserts, which was also odd to me because I had always associated savory foods with Thanksgiving.

What I Wonder

I wonder why some of these foods had such odd names and if these names were associated with a part of their culture.
I also wonder why many people began making these unusual foods at this time.

The Impacts on Me and My Community

This may actually impact the way that I’ll be eating this Thanksgiving and my diet. I feel as though this could also impact the way that people all over the country will be spending their Thanksgiving- making new foods to comfort them in these difficult times.

Catchy Headline

What Wacky Foods Are Trending In The United States?

raw_comment:
I notice a few things. For example, Hawaiian salad is the thing is Illinois, Maine has the best one (in my opinion), and I have never heard of the Pennsylvania dish, even though I've lived here my entire life. I wonder what half the things on this list are. Thanksgiving has never been  the most exciting time for me, as I don't like turkey, so I just eat pie and potatoes, not allowing me to know about that many dishes of the event.

I can't really connect this to my community, as I don't know anyone who's ever made potato filling. Then again, who knows what others are making.  All I know about is my family.

raw_comment:
I notice that many places have foods that I have never heard of. Usually on Thanksgiving, my family eats things like turkey, mashed potatoes and homemade desserts. A favorite in my extended family is ham and cheese pie, and I was surprised to find things like "Frog Eye Salad" on the map. Upon further investigation, however, I found that a lot of the things with interesting names actually sounded really good, and something I would definitely eat. 
I do, however, wonder how some of the dishes that are unfamiliar to me got their names, like the frog eye salad and the pig pickin cake, and the funeral potatoes. 
Also, I live in Pennsylvania and I have actually never heard of "Potato Filling". Is that the same as mashed potatoes? I wasn't sure. 

Map Title-  Getting Bored Of Turkey? Try Some of These Dishes Instead!

raw_comment:
I see that in my state, Pennsylvania, we have Potato Stuffing as our most searched Thanksgiving dish. Honestly, because my family celebrates Thanksgiving with different dishes and not the traditional ones, I am honestly unfamiliar with any of the other dishes that are here. We have the basics like turkey, gravy, mashed potatoes, but not cranberry relish or mirliton casserole. This may impact my community because I live in an area of Philadelphia where there are mostly immigrant Americans, and not many of us even celebrate Thanksgiving. Maybe this can inspire them to try it out and it may not be so bad after all. The impact this made on me was just that I recognized how much more dishes there are, and since these are popular searches, they must be important to Thanksgiving. I can ask my family to incorporate some of them this Thanksgiving!

I think a good, catchy headline would be:
"America is crazy about their Thanksgiving foods! Which state is your's crazy about?"

raw_comment:
1. Some of the dishes are shown several times and are usually listed next or near a similar dish, I noticed. Furthermore, most of the things listed are foods that I have not actually heard of! 

2. I wonder why with their names, a lot of these dishes seem very peculiar, very long and confusing that said out loud could cause a tongue-twister! 

3. It is very difficult to describe the effect this has on me and my community, I feel like many of the items listed above are things I would not allow my family to eat.

4. I'd call this map: Weird Foods With Bizarre Names. I genuinely understand things like maple walnut pie (which sounds delicious), but when I imagine what they actually look like, things like frog eye salad and persimmon bread sound very frankly strange and slightly disgusting!

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Labeled choropleth-style map / thematic geographic map** of U.S. states and Puerto Rico, with text labels placed over each region.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses a **geographic map layout** based on state boundaries.
   - No faceting, stacking, or small multiples.
   - Labels are placed directly on states; some crowded Northeast labels use **leader lines/callouts**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state / territory | Categorical/nominal | Geographic position/region on map |
| Dish / food name associated with each state | Categorical/nominal | Text label placed on or near each state; callout lines for some states |

**Notes:**  
- State boundaries are visible as the geographic framework.  
- No quantitative scale, color legend, or temporal variable is shown.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s map shows the “most distinct” Thanksgiving side dishes by state based on the number of Google recipe searches for the week before Thanksgiving for the period 2004 -2013.  By SELECTING THE STATE from the article (link in the release), you will see how much more distinct, on a per capita basis, this side dish and other dishes are in this state versus the rest of the country.  For example, in Colorado, frog eye salad is 14 times more commonly searched (relative to population size) than in the rest of the country.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the map. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this map and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

1. A lot of Western states have more healthy options. 
2. A lot of Eastern states have desserts as favorites 
3. States in the Midwest and the South have more uncommon foods as favorites

1. What cultural influences play a role in these stats?

Snapp Title - 
What Are American's Eating This Thanksgiving?

raw_comment:
Catchy Title: “Turkey it up: What others eat for the Thanksgiving meal”

What I noticed: I noticed that frog eye salads are popular in some states on the west coast of the U.S. at the time this survey was done, and I really think the name should be changed because there are no frog eyes in it. Snicker salad and smoked salmon dip, sound kinda delish though.

What I wonder:  Honestly from a History POV the reason why some Thanksgiving dishes are popular in states is that the dishes apply to the state’s history. Like in Florida, the popular dish is a Spanish dish.

Impact on my community, and others: This goes to show that Thanksgiving is not all about Turkey and Gravy. There are more options than the basic meal.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the United States obviously searches very strange Thanksgiving dishes on Google. I noticed that snicker salad and frog eye salad are both very popular in the Midwest. In the New England area and on the East Coast, the people there are interested in the “more commonly eaten dishes.” These dishes include foods with pumpkin, maple or chocolate—universal Thanksgiving staples. 

I am obviously wondering like everyone else, why people are searching foods that aren’t commonly eaten on Thanksgiving. Are people getting bored of eating the same things year after year? Do people want to see a change on the menu?

This might impact me in my community with grocery stores and restaurants starting to make and sell these “distinct” google-searched dishes. By looking at these searches, grocery stores and restaurants may see a demand in people wanting to eat these dishes.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

In today’s New York Times graph, Nov. 18, 2020, we are detecting what foods have high popularities in each individual state. Each place shares a unique dish that may be foreign to the others, being from Texas I’ve never heard of funeral potatoes. These potatoes include shredded hash browns, potato chips, sour cream, and chicken broth, then baked for about an hour.


What do you wonder?

I think what I’m personally questioning the most, is how these certain sides came about in each state? Is there historical context involved? Or are they foods that people usually associate with the locations? There are very intriguing names, Pig Pickin Cake, Snicker Salad, and Dirt Pudding. How were these titles decided? 


What impact does this have on you and your community?

Due to the state I live in, sopapilla cheesecake will likely make more of an appearance than something like vegan mushroom gravy, as I’ve no outside sources that could introduce these items onto my thanksgiving table. 


What’s going on in this map? Write a catchy headline that captures the map’s main idea.

People viewing this graph are learning about new delicious foods that make an entrance come Thanksgiving day for an immense amount of individuals, from smoked salmon dip to pumpkin whoopie pie. We could caption it, "Turkey enchiladas, pumpkin rolls, and 4 layer delights, oh my!"
